narrative:
Your estimated chance of failing is 16%, roughly one in six. That is a low but real risk, and under the rule used it is enough to require remedial courses as a precaution rather than a certainty.

In the model’s ranking, your record of no past class failures was the strongest factor, and it worked in your favor, lowering your estimated risk. Your intention to pursue higher education and your good family relationships were the next most influential; both also pushed toward passing. So the top signals the model highlighted are protective, not reasons to expect failure. The concern likely comes from other patterns in your profile: you study fewer than two hours a week, while passers most often study two to five; you have nine absences, compared with an average of about four among passers; and you lack internet at home, which only about one in five passers lack. These can make it harder to keep up, even when your past record and goals are positive.

To improve, raise your weekly study time, reduce absences, and arrange reliable internet or school resources. Use your family support and your goal of higher education as motivators, and ask about extra help before small gaps become serious.
